newsitem.title: UK: El Nino could cut cocoa crop by up to 300,000 T.
newsitem.headline: El Nino could cut cocoa crop by up to 300,000 T.

text.p: A strong El Nino event, the cyclical weather pattern developing in the tropical Pacific Ocean, could cut world cocoa production by between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes, according to a recent study by a UK independent consultant.
Landell Mills Commodities said that the last severe El Nino in 1982/83 -- this century's worst -- had caused Ivorian production to drop by 20 percent below its trend line.
It said globally, the crop reduction over a three-year period then (pre-El Nino, during El Nino and post-El Nino years) was 330,000 tonnes. In 1991-1992, the fall was slower at 121,000 tonnes.
LMC said if a strong El Nino strikes this time around, it could impact the crop by 200,000 to 300,000 tonnes.
Scientists have warned that the El Nino, which won't peak until December could be almost as severe as that of 1982/83.

The weather pattern is caused by the warming of the Pacific Ocean which interacts with other weather systems and typically produces freak weather such as drought in some areas and heavier than normal rainfall in others.
The 1983 El Nino caused withering drought in Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines and South Africa. Floods inundated India and Peru while severe winter storms lashed California.

UK brokerage Merill Lynch said in its latest bi-weekly report the timing was of utmost importance and crop watchers have suggested it has started too late to wreak havoc on the upcoming main crop. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
